CT vs PT: understanding the difference

Current transformers and potential transformers help meters and protection equipment work with the electrical quantities in a power system. Their names describe the key difference: one represents current, while the other represents voltage.

What does a CT do?

A current transformer, or CT, produces a secondary current related to the current in its primary circuit. This lets suitable instruments measure a much larger system current through a scaled signal. CTs are used in measurement and protection applications.

What does a PT do?

A potential transformer, or PT, is also called a voltage transformer (VT). It provides a secondary voltage related to the primary system voltage. That signal can be used by compatible meters, monitoring equipment and protection relays.

The difference at a glance

Comparing the basic purpose of CTs and PTs
FeatureCTPT / VT
Quantity representedCurrentVoltage
Secondary signalScaled currentScaled voltage
Typical roleCurrent measurement and protection inputsVoltage measurement and protection inputs

Why the application matters

Metering and protection have different performance requirements. A familiar ratio or a similar-looking housing does not establish whether a device suits the intended circuit. Accuracy, burden and the equipment it serves all matter.

For a project discussion, identify the measurement or protection function first, then share the required ratios, ratings and installation details. This gives the manufacturer a clear starting point for reviewing a suitable CT or PT.
